Aristotle. Three hundred and eighty-four to three hundred and twenty-two BCE. He was a Greek philosopher born in Macedonia who studied under Plato, founded his own school called the Lyceum, and systematized logic, metaphysics, ethics, and natural science. His belief in empirical observation, final causes, and the primacy of the individual rather than abstract forms made him the counterweight to Platonism and the architect of Western science and philosophy.

Aristotle was born in Stagira in northern Greece. He joined Plato's Academy at age seventeen and remained there for twenty years. He became tutor to the young Alexander the Great, which gave him access to Macedonia's resources and specimens. He founded the Lyceum in Athens in three hundred and thirty-five BCE. He taught while walking, so his school became known as the peripatetic school. He wrote over two hundred treatises. Most surviving works are lecture notes, fragmentary and dense.

He invented formal logic, the theory of the syllogism. If A equals B and B equals C, then A equals C. Logic was his organon—his tool for all other inquiry. This framework lasted two thousand years. He advocated empirical observation and classification. He rejected Plato's forms as unnecessary. Knowledge, he argued, comes from examining particulars and deriving universal principles from them.

His metaphysics rejected transcendence. Being is not transcendent but immanent. The form, which he called the eidos or essence, exists in the individual thing. Every thing has a telos, a final cause or purpose. Understanding nature means grasping what something is for. Matter and form are inseparable. Change happens when potential becomes actual. Natural motion—falling and rising—and celestial motion, eternal and circular, reveal divine hierarchy.

His ethics taught that virtue is a habit, not knowledge. It is the mean between extremes. Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness. Eudaimonia—flourishing, often mistranslated as happiness—is the highest good, achieved by exercising virtue. Humans are political animals. The state exists to enable human flourishing. He also defended natural slavery and gender hierarchy by appeal to nature, claims that modern philosophy rejects.

Aristotle is the most systematizing mind in ancient philosophy. His logic, metaphysics, and natural philosophy dominated Western thought through the Middle Ages and Renaissance. Even his errors persisted—geocentrism and impetus theory were so well-articulated that they endured until Galileo and Newton. His virtue ethics experienced a twentieth-century revival as an alternative to consequentialism and deontology. The breadth of his work—spanning logic, biology, politics, rhetoric, poetics—makes him the model of the universal scholar.
